t.5.46.1: Then, when Prince Akṣa had been slain by Hanumān, the great-souled lord of the Rākṣasas, steadying his mind, in his wrath commanded Indrajit, who was equal to Indra.
t.5.46.2: You, knower of divine weapons, are the foremost of those who bear arms, a bringer of grief even to the gods and asuras; your deeds have been witnessed among the gods together with Indra, and you have gathered your divine weapons by propitiating the Grandfather.
t.5.46.4: You are well guarded by the might of your arms and protected by your austerity; you know how to discern the right place and time, and you alone are foremost in wisdom.
t.5.46.3: Having met the might of your weapons in battle, neither the Asuras nor the hosts of the Maruts, nor anyone at all in the three worlds, has escaped being worn out.
t.5.46.5: There is nothing impossible for you to accomplish by your deeds in battles, and nothing beyond your doing in counsel guided by wisdom. Truly, there is no one in the three realms who does not know the might of your weapons and your strength.
t.5.46.7: All the Kiṃkaras have been slain, and the Rākṣasa Jambumālī too, as well as the heroic sons of the ministers and the five warriors who march at the head of the army.
t.5.46.6: The strength of your penance, your valor, and the power of your weapons in battle are equal to mine. Having you in the clash of battle, the mind, certain of its purpose, feels no weariness.
t.5.46.9: O wise one, having seen this great strength of the monkey, his might and his valour, and having weighed your own power as well, make an onslaught befitting your own strength.
t.5.46.8: Your beloved brother, the prince Akṣa, has been slain; yet the strength I rely on in you, O destroyer of foes, is not found in those others.
t.5.46.10: Consider your own strength and that of the enemy, and act so that, once you have drawn near and gone forth, the crushing of our army comes to rest with the enemy quelled and subdued, O best of those skilled in weapons.
t.5.46.11: Surely this is not the best of counsels, that I send you forth; yet this counsel is held to accord with the duties of kings and with the way of the kṣatriya.
t.5.46.12: O subduer of foes, skill in battle with various weapons must certainly be mastered, and victory in combat is ever to be desired.
t.5.46.13: Then, having heard those words of his father, the hero, whose might equalled that of the sons of Dakṣa, undaunted in spirit and with his mind resolved upon battle, reverently circumambulated his lord, keeping him on his right.
t.5.46.14: Then Indrajit, honored in return by those beloved companions of his own retinue, his zeal roused and fierce for the fight, set out for battle.
t.5.46.15: The glorious son of the lord of the Rākṣasas, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose splendour was great, went forth like the ocean surging on the days of the moon's changes.
t.5.46.16: Indrajit, who was like Indra himself, mounted his chariot of unimpeded speed, yoked with four beasts of prey with white, sharp fangs, whose speed equalled that of the king of birds.
t.5.46.17: That chariot-warrior, foremost among bowmen, skilled in weapons and best among those versed in missiles, swiftly advanced by chariot to where Hanūmān was.
t.5.46.18: Hearing the rumble of his chariot and the twang of his bow's string, that heroic monkey became even more greatly delighted.
t.5.46.19: Taking up a very great bow, sharp-pointed darts and arrows, the warrior skilled in battle went forth, heading toward Hanumān.
t.5.46.21: There gathered Nāgas and Yakṣas, great sages, Cakracaras and Siddhas, and flocks of birds, covering the sky, cried out loudly, supremely delighted.
t.5.46.20: Then, as he, filled with delight at the battle, went forth to the fight with arrows in hand, all the quarters of the sky grew murky, and fierce beasts howled in many ways.
t.5.46.22: Seeing Indrajit swiftly approaching with his chariot, the monkey roared a mighty roar and, full of impetuous force, grew in size.
t.5.46.24: Then those two met, both exceedingly swift and mighty, fearless in battle, the monkey and the son of the lord of the Rākṣasas, like the lords of the Suras and Asuras bound in enmity.
t.5.46.23: Indrajit, mounted on his divine chariot and bearing a wondrous bow, drew that bow taut, making it resound with a sound as mighty as lightning.
t.5.46.25: Grown mighty, that immeasurable one struck down the rushing force of the arrows of that heroic great chariot-warrior, the bowman esteemed in battle, and ranged along the path of his father, the sky.
t.5.46.27: Hearing that rattle of his chariot, the sound of the mṛdaṅgas, kettledrums and paṭahas, and the twang of his bow as it was being drawn, he sprang up again.
t.5.46.26: Then the hero, slayer of enemy heroes, loosed in close succession well-feathered arrows with long, sharp heads and gold-adorned shafts, striking with the force of a falling thunderbolt.
t.5.46.29: Again he came forward in front of his arrows; then Hanumān, the son of the Wind, stretched out his hands and leapt up.
t.5.46.28: The great monkey swiftly wheeled about in the spaces between the arrows, and so the monkey foiled the aim of the one who was targeting him.
t.5.46.30: Those two, both endowed with great speed and skilled in the work of battle, waged a supreme fight that captivated the minds of all beings.
t.5.46.31: The rākṣasa found no opening in Hanumān, nor did Māruti find an opening in that great-souled one. Having met in combat, those two, whose valor equalled that of the gods, proved irresistible to each other.
t.5.46.33: Then the son of the rākṣasa king fixed his mind on that foremost of monkey heroes. Seeing that the monkey could not be slain, he pondered how he might be brought under control, intent on capturing him.
t.5.46.34: Then that hero, the foremost of those skilled in weapons, endowed with exceedingly great splendour, fitted to his bow the weapon of the Grandsire, aiming it at that best of monkeys.
t.5.46.32: Then, as the target was being struck and the arrows kept falling in vain, that great-souled one, his mind composed through steadfast concentration, fell into deep thought.
t.5.46.35: Knowing that he could not be slain, the mighty-armed Indrajit, versed in the true nature of weapons, seized that son of Māruta with a divine weapon.
t.5.46.36: Then that monkey, bound with the weapon by that rākṣasa, became motionless and fell upon the surface of the earth.
t.5.46.38: Then Hanumān reflected upon the Brahmāstra, consecrated with the mantras of Svayambhū, and upon the boon granted to him by the Grandfather.
t.5.46.37: Then the foremost hero among the monkeys, realizing that he was bound by the weapon and that his force had dwindled through the power of the lord, reflected on the favor the Grandsire had shown to him.
t.5.46.39: I have no power to free myself from the bond of this weapon, owing to the might of the Teacher of the worlds. Thinking thus, he resolved that the bond of the Self-born's weapon, so ordained, must be submitted to by me.
t.5.46.40: The monkey, having considered the power of the weapon and the grace of the Grandsire, and having reflected on his own power to free himself, obeyed the command of the Grandsire.
t.5.46.41: Even though I am bound by the weapon, no fear arises in me, for I am protected by Pitāmaha and Mahendra, and by Anila as well.
t.5.46.42: Even in being seized by the rākṣasas I see a great advantage for myself: a conversation with the lord of the rākṣasas. Therefore let the enemies take me.
t.5.46.44: Then the Rākṣasas, seeing that tamer of foes motionless, bound him with ropes of hemp-bark and with strips of tree-bark twisted tightly together.
t.5.46.43: He, firm in his purpose, a slayer of enemy heroes who acts only after due reflection, ceased his struggling; seized by the foes who had forcibly rushed upon him, and reviled by each of them in turn, he roared aloud.
t.5.46.45: He was willing to be bound by the enemy and forcibly seized by their heroes, his purpose fixed on this thought: “Perhaps the lord of the rākṣasas, out of curiosity, will resolve to see me.”
t.5.46.46: Bound with that bark rope, the mighty one was freed from the weapon, for the binding of a divine weapon does not persist alongside any other bond.
t.5.46.47: Then the heroic Indrajit, seeing that foremost of monkeys bound with cords of tree-bark and released from the astra, fell into anxious thought, for when one is bound by another bond, the astra gives way.
t.5.46.48: Alas, a great deed has been rendered fruitless, for the rākṣasas did not consider the working of the mantra. Once a weapon has been nullified, no other weapon takes effect again; we are all now in peril.
t.5.46.49: Hanumān, released by the weapon, does not realize that he is free, for he is being dragged along by the rākṣasas and is tightly pressed by those bonds.
t.5.46.50: Then, being beaten by the cruel rākṣasas with sticks and fists, that monkey was dragged into the presence of the lord of the rākṣasas.
t.5.46.51: Then Indrajit, seeing that he had been released by the weapon and was bound with cords of tree-bark, presented that mighty foremost of monkeys there to the king and his retinue.
t.5.46.53: "Who is this? Whose is he, and from where has he come? What is his purpose, and who is his support?" Such were the talks that arose there among the heroic Rākṣasas.
t.5.46.52: The rākṣasas presented that foremost of the best of monkeys, bound like a maddened elephant, to Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas.
t.5.46.54: Then other rākṣasas there, greatly enraged, said to one another, "Let him be killed, or let him be burned, or let him be devoured!"
t.5.46.55: Having swiftly passed along the road, the great-souled one saw there, at the feet of the lord of the rākṣasas, the king's aged attendants and the hall adorned with great jewels.
t.5.46.56: That greatly radiant Rāvaṇa beheld the best of monkeys being dragged hither and thither by rākṣasas of hideous form.
t.5.46.57: And the best of monkeys also beheld the lord of the rākṣasas, endowed with splendor and strength, like the blazing sun.
t.5.46.59: And the monkey, questioned by them in due order about the purpose of his errand and, first of all, the root of the matter, declared: "I have come as a messenger from the presence of the lord of the monkeys."
t.5.46.58: Then Daśānana, his copper-red eyes rolling with rage, gazed at that monkey and gave orders concerning him to his chief counsellors seated there, men eminent in lineage and character.
